name: Mogalrajapuram Caves
deity: Shiva; Cave II holds sanctums for Brahma, Shiva and Vishnu
significance: A group of five rock-cut cave shrines on a hill in eastern Vijayawada, excavated around the 7th century and variously credited to the Vishnukundins or the early Eastern Chalukyas. Cave II is the most developed of them, with Shiva as Nataraja and Ardhanarisvara among its carvings; the site is centrally protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Bumzuva Cave and Temple
deity: Shiva (Shivalinga)
significance: A carved limestone cave with an attached stone temple above the Bavan springs in the Lidder valley of Anantnag district, believed to date from the 12th century and protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. Two shrines at the foot of the cave were later converted into Muslim ziarats, the larger one to Baba Bandin Sahib, a disciple of Shaikh Nuruddin.

name: Vizhinjam Cave Temple
deity: Vinadhara Dakshinamurti (Shiva)
significance: A one-celled granite cave shrine at Vizhinjam, the port that served as headquarters of the Ay kings of southern Kerala in the 8th century. Its outer wall carries reliefs of Shiva that were left unfinished, worked in the Pallava manner of the period.

name: Vijayalaya Choleeswaram
deity: Shiva
significance: A hill temple at Narthamalai combining rock-cut and structural Dravida work, raised in 862 CE by Sattan Paliyili, a lieutenant of the Muttaraiyar chiefs who held the region as Pallava feudatories. Damaged by rain and lightning, it was restored under Tennavan Tamiladirayan and is now an Archaeological Survey of India protected monument.

name: Ramalingeshwara Group of Temples, Avani
deity: Ramalingeshwara (Shiva)
dynasty: Nolamba, with Chola and Vijayanagara additions
significance: A walled group of Shaiva shrines at Avani in Kolar district, its four principal lingas named for Rama, Lakshmana, Bharata and Shatrughna, with further shrines to Vali, Sugriva and Parvati. An inscription of 399 CE refers to the site, later ones call it the Gaya of the south, and the ornate 10th-century Nolamba work was renovated by the Cholas before the Vijayanagara kings added the main mandapa and rajagopura.
story: Tradition holds that Rama halted at Avani on his return from Lanka, and that his sons Lava and Kusha were born on the hill nearby that still bears their name.

name: Markanda Mahadev Temples
place: Markanda Deo, Chamorshi taluka, Gadchiroli district
deity: Shiva (Markandeshwar)
significance: A forty-acre group of Shiva temples near Chamorshi in Gadchiroli district, attributed to the Rashtrakutas who held the region from the 8th to the 12th century. The carved figures covering its outer walls have earned it the local name of a mini Khajuraho, though many of the shrines now stand dilapidated.
story: The place is named for the sage Markandeya, who is said to have performed penance on the river bank here and, when he moved to offer up his own life, was stopped by Shiva, who blessed him and gave the temple his name.

name: Brindaban Chandra's Math
deity: Brindabanchandra (Radha-Krishna); also Chaitanya-Nityananda, Rama and Krishnachandra
significance: A Vaishnava math at Guptipara in Hooghly district holding four temples — Chaitanyadev, Brindabanchandra, Ramchandra and Krishnachandra. The scholar David McCutchion identified its Chaitanya temple, of Akbar's reign, as the earliest Bangla-style temple still standing, and the Ramchandra temple carries a rich terracotta facade; the complex is an ASI-listed monument.

name: Jor Mandir
deity: Narayana
significance: A north-south row of three ek-ratna brick temples at Bishnupur, built in 1726 by Gopal Singha Dev I of Mallabhum, the largest of them richly ornamented in stucco with scenes from the Ramayana and the Krishna-lila. The group is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India and has stood on UNESCO's World Heritage tentative list since 1998.

name: Group of Temples at Magadi
deity: Ranganatha (Vishnu) and Someshwara (Shiva)
dynasty: Chola, with Vijayanagara and Kempe Gowda additions
significance: Two state-protected temples in the town of Magadi, about 41 km from Bangalore: the Ranganatha temple, consecrated under a Chola ruler in the early 12th century and given its gopuras by Krishnadeva Raya in 1524, and the Someshwara temple raised by the Kempe Gowda line. Magadi is the birthplace of Kempe Gowda, the Vijayanagara chieftain who founded Bangalore.
story: The presiding image is said to have been installed by the sage Mandavya, from whom the place takes its name of Mandavya Kshetra, and a small figure of Ranganatha on the temple wall is believed to grow a little larger every year.

name: Uppatasanti Pagoda
deity: Gautama Buddha (tooth relic; four jade Buddha images)
significance: A large stupa in Myanmar's purpose-built capital Naypyidaw, begun in November 2006 and consecrated in March 2009 under Than Shwe of the ruling State Peace and Development Council. Built as a near same-sized replica of the Shwedagon Pagoda, it enshrines a Buddha tooth relic and houses four jade Buddha images.
story: Its name, meaning protection against calamity, comes from a sutta composed by a monk in the early 16th century and recited in times of crisis, above all in the face of foreign invasion.

name: Alaungdaw Kathapa Pagoda
deity: Mahakassapa, a chief disciple of the Buddha
significance: A Theravada pagoda at the centre of Alaungdaw Kathapa National Park in Kani township, Sagaing Region, and the park's namesake. Pilgrims gather there for annual festivals held in fixed lunar months.
story: Local lore holds that the cave at the pagoda contains the preserved remains of Mahakassapa, one of the Buddha's principal disciples.

name: Peace Pagoda, Darjeeling
deity: Four avatars of the Buddha, including Maitreya
significance: One of the Nipponzan-Myohoji peace pagodas, 28.5 m high and 23 m across, on the slopes of Jalapahar hill at Darjeeling. Its foundation stone was laid in 1972 under the Japanese monk Nichidatsu Fujii, it was designed by M. Ohka, and it was inaugurated in 1992 as a focus for people of all races and creeds seeking world peace.

name: Dhammayazika Pagoda
deity: Maitreya, the future Buddha, in one of five shrines
significance: A circular brick pagoda of three terraces at Pwasaw east of Bagan, built in 1196 in the reign of King Narapatisithu. It is laid out on a pentagon with five shrines instead of the usual four — the oldest known building with fivefold rotational symmetry — and its terracotta tiles illustrate scenes from the Jataka.

name: Bupaya Pagoda
deity: Gautama Buddha (relics of the Buddha)
dynasty: Modern rebuild, traditionally ascribed to Pyusawhti
significance: A gilded bulbous stupa on diminishing terraces overlooking the Irrawaddy at Bagan, enshrining relics of the Buddha. Its date is disputed, claims ranging from the 2nd to the 11th century; the original collapsed into the river in the 1975 Bagan earthquake and was rebuilt in reinforced concrete between 1976 and 1978.
story: The name joins bu, a gourd, to paya, a pagoda: the young Pyusawhti is said to have destroyed five great menaces, among them a rampant gourd creeper on this spot, and to have raised a pagoda wherever he overcame one.

name: Phra Mahathat Kaen Nakhon
deity: Relics of the Buddha, kept in crystal containers
builtDisplay: wat founded 1789; stupa for King Bhumibol's Golden Jubilee
significance: A nine-storey stupa 80 m high on a square base of 50 m at Wat Nong Waeng beside the Kaen Nakhon marsh in Khon Kaen, raised to mark the Golden Jubilee of King Bhumibol Adulyadej and the bicentenary of the province, and modelled on Phra That Kham Kaen. The wat itself was founded in 1789 by Thao Pia Mueang Pan, was left as the old town when the city moved in 1811, and was approved as a royal temple in 1984.

name: Hoằng Phúc Temple
place: Thuan Trach, My Thuy commune, Le Thuy district
deity: Gautama Buddha (sarira relics from the Shwedagon Pagoda)
significance: One of the oldest temples in central Vietnam, with a history of more than 700 years. Founded as Tri Kien Temple and visited by Emperor Tran Nhan Tong by 1301, it was renamed Kinh Thien Tu in 1716 by Nguyen Phuc Chu and Hoang Phuc Tu in 1821 by Minh Mang; wrecked by a hurricane in 1985, it was rebuilt from December 2014, reopened in January 2016 with relics presented by the Myanmar Sangha, and is a recognised national historical relic.

name: Setkyathiha Pagoda
deity: Gautama Buddha (bronze image cast for King Bagyidaw)
significance: A pagoda south of Zegyo market on the east bank of the Shwetachaung canal in Mandalay, completed in 1884 to house a large bronze Buddha cast at Inwa for King Bagyidaw before 1824. The image was moved to Amarapura in 1852 at the outbreak of the Second Anglo-Burmese War and on to Mandalay in 1885 with the Third.

name: Myathalun Pagoda
deity: Gautama Buddha (the Bed of the Buddha enshrined within)
significance: The principal pagoda of Magway in central Myanmar. Raised from its original 55.5 feet to 87 feet by the Bagan king Saw Lu (1077-1084), it was badly damaged in the earthquake of 1847 and rebuilt to about 104 feet by the mayor Min Din Min Hla Kyaw Gaung.
story: Legend holds that the pagoda was first built by a wealthy man called U Baw Gyaw and his wife.

name: Lokahteikpan Temple
deity: Seated Gautama Buddha
significance: A small brick temple at Bagan founded about 1125 in the reign of King Alaungsithu, with a seated Buddha image in its central hall. Its murals of the five hundred and fifty Jatakas carry captions in Mon and Old Burmese that are among the earliest surviving examples of the Old Burmese script.

name: Shanti Stupa, Pokhara
deity: Relics of the Buddha, with four statues of scenes from his life
significance: Nepal's first World Peace Pagoda, a white stupa 115 feet high on Anadu hill at 1,100 m above Pokhara, built by the Nipponzan-Myohoji monk Morioka Sonin with local supporters including Dharmashilla Guruma and Min Bahadur Gurung. Nichidatsu Fujii laid the foundation stone in September 1973; work was obstructed for eighteen years and builders were repeatedly arrested, until the stone was re-laid in 1992 by prime minister Girija Prasad Koirala and the stupa was completed in October 1999.

name: Hsinbyume Pagoda
deity: Dedicated to the memory of Princess Hsinbyume (1789-1812)
significance: A white terraced pagoda at Mingun, built in 1816 by King Bagyidaw in memory of his first consort and cousin Princess Hsinbyume, who had died in childbirth nearby. Its form is a marked departure from Burmese pagoda norms; King Mindon restored it in 1874 after the earthquake of 1839, and it was badly damaged again in the 2025 Myanmar earthquake.
story: It is modelled on the mythical Sulamani pagoda that stands atop Mount Meru, its seven concentric terraces representing the seven mountain ranges that ring the sacred mountain in Buddhist cosmology.

name: Lawkananda Pagoda
deity: Gautama Buddha (replica of a tooth relic)
significance: A stupa on the bank of the Ayeyarwady at Bagan, built in the reign of King Anawrahta, founder of the Pagan Empire, and holding a replica of a tooth relic of the Buddha. A bejewelled hti was hoisted to its summit on 24 May 2003, and its annual festival falls in July.

name: Silver Pagoda
place: Royal Palace, Chey Chumneas, Phnom Penh
deity: The Emerald Buddha of green crystal, and a life-size gold Maitreya Buddha
significance: The royal temple within the Royal Palace compound at Phnom Penh, completed in the 19th century under King Norodom and later remodelled under Norodom Sihanouk with 5,329 silver floor tiles and Italian marble. It holds a small green crystal Buddha and a life-size gold Maitreya of 90 kg set with 9,584 diamonds, made in the palace workshops in 1906-07; Sihanouk was ordained there on 31 July 1947, and the Maitreya lost most of its diamonds during the civil war before restorations from 1985.
story: The Reamker, the Khmer telling of the Ramayana, runs in murals along 642 m of the enclosing wall, and the legend of Preah Ko Preah Keo is represented by two statues.

name: Umin Thonze Pagoda
deity: Gautama Buddha (45 seated Buddha images)
dynasty: Konbaung rebuild, founded under the Sagaing Kingdom
significance: A shrine cut into the Sagaing Hills holding 45 seated Buddha images set in a curve against sparkling glasswork. Founded in the 1330s by King Tarabya I of Sagaing and renovated in 1643 and 1723, it was severely damaged by the earthquake of 1838 and rebuilt by King Pagan Min, the work completed in 1847.

name: Nan Oo Pagoda, Myinsaing
deity: Commemorative stupa of the Burmese victory over the Mongols in 1301
significance: A pagoda beside the Myinsaing palace site, founded in 1301 by Athinkhaya to commemorate the Burmese victory over the Mongols. King Uzana I of Pinya enveloped the original completely within a larger structure in 1329/30, following an earlier project at Mekkhaya; the fabric had badly decayed by 1925 and restoration was completed in 2004.

name: Kyaikhtisaung Pagoda
deity: Hair relic and tooth relic of Gautama Buddha
significance: A hill pagoda in Bilin township, Mon State, said to enshrine a hair relic of the Buddha, with a tooth relic added under King Culasirimasoka. Long neglected, its hti came to lean — giving the name Kyaik Htisaung, the pagoda with the tilting umbrella — until the monk U Pannadipa returned in 1971 and led four decades of rebuilding across nine shrines.
story: Tradition tells that Gautama Buddha came to Kaylartha mountain and gave strands of his hair to hermits, monks and two belu brothers, Deiwa Kondala and Namani Kondala, who raised the pagoda to enshrine them.

name: Shwemawdaw Pagoda
deity: Two hair relics of the Buddha, with a tooth relic added in 982/83
dynasty: Modern rebuild, Hanthawaddy and Konbaung antecedents
significance: The great stupa of Bago, capital of Hanthawaddy, enshrining hair relics of the Buddha with a tooth relic added in 982/83. Donald Stadtner notes that its founding tradition surfaces only in the late 18th century, while documentation begins in the late 14th: Razadarit ringed it with 160 small stupas in 1390 and Bayinnaung gave it a jewelled hti in 1556; Bodawpaya raised it to 90 m in 1796, earthquakes in 1912, 1917 and 1930 wrecked it, and repairs were completed in 1954.
story: Tradition holds that the merchant brothers Kullasala and Mahasala received two strands of hair from the Buddha himself and raised the first stupa over them.

name: Mahazedi Pagoda
deity: Gautama Buddha (a gold and jewel-encrusted replica of the tooth relic)
significance: A pagoda at Bago built by King Bayinnaung between November 1559 and May 1560, its hti raised on 2 January 1561, to house a gold and jewel-encrusted replica of the Buddha's tooth given by Dharmapala of Kotte. The relics arrived in 1576, were carried off to Taungoo by Anaukpetlun in 1599 and on to the Kaunghmudaw at Inwa by Thalun in 1636; earthquakes on the Sagaing fault damaged the stupa in 1564, 1583 and 1888, levelled it in 1930, and it was rebuilt in the 1950s.
